subject: Pricing guardrails: floor/ceiling alignment and fallback plan
body:
From: Grace Lee <glee@acmeanalytics.com>
To: Jordan Blake <jordan_blake@redwood.com>
Cc: procurement@acmeanalytics.com
Date: 2026-09-29 07:45 PDT
Subject: Pricing guardrails: floor/ceiling alignment and fallback plan

Jordan —

Attached are Acme's annotated redlines for Exhibit A (pricing schedule). The key items we want to resolve before procurement signs:

- "Floor" definition: We need the floor to be expressed as an annualized committed-minimum with true-up mechanics (quarterly). The current draft language could be read as a monthly minimum, which creates cash-flow mismatch for us.
- "Ceiling" enforcement: We are asking for a hard monthly ceiling (to cap cost exposure) paired with automatic throttling to avoid outages.
- Fallback behavior: If Redwood auto-throttles, we need clearly defined SLA credits and a deterministic re-route/failover path so our product doesn't degrade silently.

I'm sending Acme_Pricing_Redlines_v3.pdf (see attachment). Can we do a quick call today (PST) to align on language? If useful I've looped in our CPO, Tom Rivers.

Best,
Grace Lee
Senior Counsel, Acme Analytics
[Attachment: Acme_Pricing_Redlines_v3.pdf (PDF, 42KB)]

---
From: Jordan Blake <jordan_blake@redwood.com>
To: Grace Lee <glee@acmeanalytics.com>
Cc: lauren_bishop@redwood.com
Date: 2026-09-29 08:12 PDT
Subject: Re: Pricing guardrails: floor/ceiling alignment and fallback plan

Thanks Grace — and thanks for the detailed markup. I can take a call at 9:30am PST.

High-level responses before we chat:
- Floor: We intended the floor to be an annualized commit with quarterly true-up. Happy to make that explicit language.
- Ceiling/throttle: Our product has two levers — a hard per-account token cap and an operational rate limiter that can be applied per-route. A hard monthly ceiling as you describe is doable, but it materially increases our per-unit pricing unless paired with a usage band for burst capacity.
- SLA credits: we generally provide credits tied to region/availability breaches. We can extend the definition to include throttling incidents if it's clearly defined.

Can you confirm whether Acme expects bursts above the monthly ceiling to be denied outright (error responses) or queued/throttled with a best-effort degrade? That affects the wording.

Jordan Blake
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
Mobile: +1 (415) 555-0198

---
From: Grace Lee <glee@acmeanalytics.com>
To: Jordan Blake <jordan_blake@redwood.com>, procurement@acmeanalytics.com
Date: 2026-09-29 09:05 PDT
Subject: Re: Pricing guardrails: floor/ceiling alignment and fallback plan

Jordan —

Thanks. Short answers:
- Bursts: we want throttling (best-effort) rather than hard errors. Quiet failures are bad — if requests are queued/delayed we need explicit headers indicating degraded mode and a documented fallback to our internal cached path.
- Credits: If throttling results from capacity constraints when utilization > 90% for > 10 minutes, we want a credit equal to X% of the token cost for that window.

I've attached a marked-up paragraph for the fallback section. Tom is on copy to confirm the risk tolerance.

Grace

---
From: Jordan Blake <jordan_blake@redwood.com>
To: lauren_bishop@redwood.com, marissa_cole@redwood.com
Date: 2026-09-29 09:30 PDT
Subject: Fwd: Pricing guardrails: floor/ceiling alignment and fallback plan

Internal — quick alignment before the call with Acme (9:30). Key asks from Acme above. My read and proposed negotiation approach:

1) Make the "floor" explicit as annualized with quarterly true-ups. This is a low-cost concession that reduces ambiguity.
2) For the "ceiling" propose a two-tiered model:
   - Soft ceiling: up to 110% of monthly budget where requests are rate-limited but allowed; overage billed at negotiated burst rate.
   - Hard protective cap: emergency throttle that returns 429 only if account-level throughput exceeds sustained emergency thresholds (very rare).
3) Fallback & credits: Tie credit eligibility to observable metrics we can measure: host-level utilization and queue-depth. Offer a credit matrix (0.5%–5% token credit) based on minutes of degraded throughput.

Negotiation levers: offer a temporary 10% discount on the burst rate for the first 2 quarters if they accept the soft-ceiling approach. Avoid embedding complex engineering runbooks into the contract — refer to operational playbook (console runbook link).

Marissa — can you draft compromise redline language for Exhibit A (pricing schedule) that implements (1)-(3) above? Lauren — can you confirm if legal is comfortable with credit matrix expressed as percentage of billed token cost vs. fixed dollar amount?

Thanks —
Jordan

---
From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
To: Jordan Blake <jordan_blake@redwood.com>, lauren_bishop@redwood.com
Date: 2026-09-29 09:48 PDT
Subject: Re: Fwd: Pricing guardrails: floor/ceiling alignment and fallback plan

Jordan / Lauren —

Draft compromise language (Exhibit A — Pricing Schedule):

"Floor: Customer Commit. The Customer shall commit to an Annual Minimum Commitment ('AMC') equal to the sum of monthly minimums set forth in the Order Form, with a quarterly true‑up. Failure to meet the AMC will trigger the true‑up calculation described in Section 3.2.

Ceiling and Burst Handling: Soft Ceiling. Redwood will apply a Soft Ceiling equal to 110% of the Customer's Monthly Budget. During periods where usage is between 100% and 110% of the Monthly Budget, Redwood will continue to serve requests and apply the Burst Rate as set forth in the Order Form. Hard Protective Cap. If account throughput exceeds 200% of contracted average throughput for longer than twenty (20) minutes, Redwood may apply protective throttling (429 responses) to maintain cluster stability.

Fallback & Credits: Throttling Credits. If Protected Throttling occurs as a result of capacity constraints (host utilization > 90% and queue depth > threshold) for more than ten (10) consecutive minutes, Customer may be eligible for a Service Credit equal to 1% of the token charges for each ten (10) minute interval of Protected Throttling, up to a maximum of 5% for a single calendar month. Credits are applied to the next invoice and are Customer's sole and exclusive remedy for throttling events.

Operational Notes: The Parties agree to rely on Redwood's operational playbook (referenced in the Order Form) for detailed failover steps. Any permanent changes to throttling thresholds or credit triggers must be mutually agreed in writing."
This keeps things measurable and caps financial exposure on our side. I can drop that into Draft_OrderForm_ExhibitA_v4.docx and send for review. Suggest we hold firm on the 200%/20 minute emergency threshold — that's an engineering guardrail.

Marissa
Director, Contracts
Redwood Inference

Grace —

Appreciate the quick turnaround and the clarity. Based on our call and internal review we've prepared a compromise redline for Exhibit A (see excerpt below) and uploaded a draft Order Form (Draft_OrderForm_ExhibitA_v4.docx) to the DocuSign envelope. Link: https://docusign.com/embedded/abcd1234

Excerpt (proposed):
- "Annual Minimum Commitment with quarterly true-up" (explicit language added).
- "Soft Ceiling at 110% of Monthly Budget with Burst Rate; Hard Protective Cap at emergency threshold (200% sustained for >20 minutes) that may trigger protective throttling)."
- "Throttling Credits: 1% token-credit per 10-minute interval of Protected Throttling (host utilization >90% and queue depth threshold), capped at 5% per calendar month; credits applied to following invoice; exclusive remedy)."

Commercial concession: to lower the material impact of the ceiling, we are offering an introductory 10% discount on the Burst Rate for the first two quarters following contract signature (applies to usage between 100%–110% of Monthly Budget).

If Acme is comfortable with the above, please sign the Order Form via the DocuSign link. If you prefer a short call to finalize wording, I'm happy to schedule.

Thanks —
Jordan Blake
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
